stories.title: A Family Lost Over $130,000 When Their Contractor Vanished
stories.headline_kid: A Singapore family paid a contractor to fix up their home, but he disappeared halfway through the job — here's what went wrong.
summary: Imagine saving up your pocket money for a new bicycle, giving it to a shop to order the bike, and then the shop just disappears with your money! Something similar happened to a Singapore family, except with a much bigger amount — more than S$130,000. They hired a contractor to renovate their HDB flat, which means making it look new with new floors, walls and fittings.

At first, things seemed fine. But slowly, the contractor started asking for more and more money than what was first agreed, and the work kept stopping and starting. Eventually, he stopped replying to their calls and messages completely, leaving the renovation unfinished.

This story is a warning for every family thinking of renovating their home. Experts say families should watch out for 'red flags' — warning signs like sudden extra charges, strange requests for payment, or work that keeps getting delayed without a good reason.
The lesson? Always check that a contractor is properly licensed, get everything written down in a contract, and never pay large sums of money all at once before work is done.

lenses.me: If your family ever renovates your room or house, you might overhear your parents talking about contracts and contractors — now you'll understand why they're so careful!
lenses.family: This story reminds families to read contracts carefully and never rush into paying large amounts of money without proof of work done.
lenses.friends: You could share this story with friends whose families are planning to renovate, so they know what red flags to look out for.
lenses.nation: It shows why Singapore has consumer protection rules, and why authorities keep encouraging people to check contractor credentials before hiring them.
lenses.world: Scams involving unfinished work or vanishing service providers happen in many countries, not just Singapore — being a smart, careful customer is a useful life skill everywhere.

stories.title: Malaysia's Former Leader Moves From Jail to House Arrest
stories.headline_kid: Malaysia's former prime minister Najib Razak will now serve the rest of his jail sentence at home instead of in prison.
summary: Najib Razak used to be the Prime Minister of Malaysia, our neighbouring country. Years ago, he was found guilty in court of corruption — that means using his power to take money that wasn't his — connected to a huge financial scandal called 1MDB. He was sent to prison for six years.

This week, Malaysia's Pardons Board, a group led by the Malaysian king that can reduce punishments, decided that Najib can now serve the rest of his sentence at home instead of behind bars. This is called 'house arrest'. But there's a catch: he must first pay a huge fine of about RM50 million (around US$12.26 million).

Experts say this has never happened before in Malaysia — no other convicted prisoner has been allowed to swap jail for house arrest like this. It puts Malaysia's current Prime Minister, Anwar Ibrahim, in an awkward position, because he had promised to fight corruption strongly.

Since Malaysia is right next door to Singapore, many people here are watching closely, because political changes and public trust in our neighbour can affect trade, travel and relations between the two countries.

lenses.me: You might hear grown-ups discussing this at the dinner table — it's a good chance to ask them what 'corruption' and 'pardon' mean.
lenses.family: Your family might talk about how leaders should be treated fairly, whether rich or poor, when they break the law.
lenses.friends: You and your classmates from Malaysian backgrounds might have different views — it's an interesting topic for respectful discussion.
lenses.nation: Malaysia is Singapore's closest neighbour, so political stability there matters for trade, the Causeway, and cross-border relationships.
lenses.world: This case raises a question many countries face: should powerful people get special treatment when punished for crimes?

stories.title: Divers Search Sunken Ferry as More Bodies Are Found
stories.headline_kid: A passenger ship sank in the sea near Indonesia, and divers are now working hard to find over 100 people still missing.
summary: Last weekend, a large passenger ship called Virgo Transport 8 flipped over and sank in the Java Sea, near Indonesia, while sailing between two cities. So far, nine people have been confirmed dead, and 108 survivors have been rescued safely.

Sadly, 126 passengers are still missing. Indonesian navy divers have now recovered three bodies from inside the sunken ship, and rescuers are trying a difficult and dangerous task — turning the capsized ship right-side up so they can search inside more safely.
This job is extremely tricky. Strong underwater currents, high water pressure, and the shape of the ship's hull (its body) have made it hard for divers to get in and search for survivors or bodies.

Many Singaporeans travel by ferry to nearby Indonesian islands like Batam and Bintan for holidays, so stories like this remind travellers everywhere about the importance of ship safety checks and following safety instructions on board.

lenses.me: If you ever go on a ferry ride during a family holiday, this story shows why it's important to listen carefully to safety briefings.
lenses.family: Families planning ferry trips to nearby islands might feel extra cautious and check safety records before booking tickets.
lenses.friends: You could talk to friends about what to do if there's ever an emergency on a boat or ship.
lenses.nation: Singapore's own ferry terminals and operators are reminded to keep strict safety checks, since our region has busy sea traffic.
lenses.world: This tragedy highlights how important proper ship maintenance and rescue readiness are for countries with a lot of sea travel, like Indonesia and Singapore.

stories.title: Japan Raises Interest Rates to Highest Level in 31 Years
stories.headline_kid: Japan just made borrowing money more expensive — and it could change how much your family's Japan holiday costs.
summary: Japan's central bank, called the Bank of Japan, decided to raise its interest rate to 1.25%. That may sound small, but it's the highest it's been in 31 years! An interest rate is like a 'price' for borrowing money — when it goes up, borrowing becomes more expensive, but saving money can earn a little more too.

The bank raised the rate because prices in Japan (called inflation) have been rising, and they want to keep prices under control, a bit like a school putting a strict limit on canteen prices so things don't get too expensive.

One big effect: Japan's currency, the yen, could get stronger. If the yen becomes stronger against the Singapore dollar, things bought in Japan — like sushi, toys or hotel stays — could cost Singaporean tourists a bit more than before.

Economists believe the Bank of Japan will likely keep raising rates carefully over time, which many Singaporean families planning holidays to Japan, or businesses trading with Japan, will want to watch closely.

lenses.me: If your family is planning a trip to Japan, this news could affect how much pocket money you get to spend there!
lenses.family: Parents might need to budget a little more carefully for holidays or shopping from Japan if the yen gets stronger.
lenses.friends: You could compare notes with friends about whether their families are planning Japan trips and how prices might change.
lenses.nation: Singapore businesses that trade with Japan, like importers of Japanese food or electronics, may see changes in costs.
lenses.world: Japan's decision shows how central banks around the world are trying to balance rising prices with keeping economies steady.

stories.title: Tennis Star Alex Eala Says Singapore Feels Like Home
stories.headline_kid: Rising tennis star Alexandra Eala is in Singapore for the Singapore Tennis Open, and she hopes to inspire young girls across Asia.
summary: Alexandra Eala, a 21-year-old tennis player from the Philippines, has arrived in Singapore ahead of the Singapore Tennis Open. It's been an incredible year for her — she's had many exciting wins that have made her one of Asia's most exciting young tennis stars.

In an interview, Eala shared that Singapore feels like 'one of her many homes', since she has visited and played here often. She spoke about how she's learning to handle her growing fame, while staying focused on her tennis training.

Eala also talked about wanting to inspire young women across Asia to take up sports confidently. She hopes that seeing someone from a neighbouring Southeast Asian country do well on the world stage will encourage more girls to chase their sporting dreams.
For Singapore, hosting the Singapore Tennis Open means local tennis fans get a rare chance to watch top international players compete live, right here at home.

lenses.family: Your family might enjoy watching the Singapore Tennis Open together, cheering for players from all over Asia.
lenses.friends: You could talk with friends about which sports stars inspire you and why.
lenses.nation: Singapore gets to be part of the excitement by hosting major sporting events, which brings visitors and puts our country on the sports map.
